extracted.intended_audience: physicians, coroners, medical examiners, and medical practitioners performing death/forensic examinations
extracted.subtask_description: Practical medical/forensic guidelines and tests to distinguish real death from apparent death using observable signs and artificial provocation of vital processes (respiratory, innervation, circulatory). Includes procedures, expected reactions, limitations, and distinguishing features of post-mortem vs vital phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-mortem vesication vs vital (physiological) vesication
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish vesicles produced by vital congestion from spurious/post-mortem vesicles: vital vesicles arise from exudation of a fibrino-albuminous solution coagulable by heat and are accompanied by underlying cutis that shows active congestion; post-mortem vesicles usually contain gaseous decomposition products or serum and are purely physical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On removing loosely adherent cuticle, the underlying cutis after death is 'yellowish-white, crisp, horny' in contrast to the efilorescence of vital congestion which can be repeatedly displaced and renewed by pressure. Note that heat can produce a spurious vesicle on a dead subject, but the contents and underlying tissue appearance differ from the vital process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor mortis and putrefaction as decisive post-mortem signs (with caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: When rigor mortis and putrefaction are actually established they may be accepted as infallible indications of death: rigidity (stiffening of muscles resisting joint flexion) followed by putrefactive bluish-green discoloration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of potential confounders: extreme cold can produce stiffening but frozen limbs yield a creaking noise on forced flexion; spasms resume their morbid position on removal of correcting force. Putrefactive discoloration may resemble gangrene during life but living gangrene will show a line of displaceable redness at the edge. Sequence: muscles of jaw and neck usually first in rigor, lower extremities last.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of superficial/cadaveric signs, auscultation, and ocular tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Cadaveric appearance, coldness, lividity, cessation of heart sounds by auscultation, and absence of perceptible respiratory chest movement are not always constant or unequivocal signs of death and may be misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cessation of the heart's action beyond five minutes is undoubted evidence, but acoustic detection may be fallacious in delicate cases. Ocular experiments (pupillary reaction, ophthalmoscopic fundus changes) are of comparative unimportance to general vitality. Local ligature may occlude a limb's vessels without fatality. Do not rely solely on these observations—proceed to artificial provocation tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: demonstrate minimum activity of each essential vital process
rubrics_metrics.description: The possibility of absolutely deciding vitality depends on artificial means to sensibly demonstrate the minimum activity of each essentially vital process; utter negation of specific reactions under appropriate tests is infallible evidence of death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Available measures (respiratory, innervation, circulatory tests) differ in simplicity and ease of application but, when properly carried out, yield conclusive results. Use a combination of appropriate tests rather than any single superficial sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respiratory (carbonic acid) test using lime-water
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in the most reduced state of vitality carbonic acid (CO2) is produced and extricated through the air-passages; collection of exhaled air into clear lime-water will detect CO2 by turning the lime-water opaque/milky on shaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow a few hours to elapse after apparent death so that equilibrium may be established between CO2 in the air-chambers and atmospheric air. Collect exhaled air at the anterior opening of the air-passages into a small transparent vessel containing clear lime-water. If any vital action continues, CO2 expired from the air-passages in a given time will far exceed cutaneous transpiration; lime-water will immediately become milky on shaking. Compare with expected cutaneous transpiration: in true death exhaled amount corresponds to skin transpiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innervation (electrification) test of nervo-muscular contractility
rubrics_metrics.description: Nervo-muscular contraction can be sensibly excited by repeated transmission of intense electric currents during even the feeblest vitality; utter failure to elicit contraction in muscles essential to life affords conclusive evidence of death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electrify muscles whose activity is essential to life. The glottis presents a favorable site: observe rima glottidis via laryngoscope before and during electrification—during life inspiration widens the aperture; after death the rima is elongated and narrow. If properly directed intense electric currents fail to produce responsive widening/contraction, death is certain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulatory (cutaneous capillary reactivity) test using heat, cupping, candle, inverted glass
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to excite active congestion of the cutaneous capillaries (topical irritants) yields decisive results: in a living subject mild heat or cupping induces an active, recurrent capillary congestion; in death there is an entire absence of such physiological reactions and only physical changes occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is preeminently the best test because it requires only simple appliances. Operate over the heart where skin retains warmth longest; corroborate by testing other trunk areas. Methods: hold flame close to (not touching) skin to detach cuticle—dead tissue beneath appears crisp yellowish-white and unaffected by pressure; living tissue shows readily perceptible vital redness displaceable and renewable by alternating pressure. Use a bright light and magnifying glass for inspection. Inverted-glass test: burn paper soaked in alcohol inside a glass inverted over skin—if any vitality remains a superficial capillary congestion with recurrent character will be induced; absolute inability to produce such a reaction across the trunk is infallible evidence of death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish physical vs physiological reactions to irritants
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical alterations produced on dead tissue by potent agents differ from the comprehensive physiological active congestion seen in life; e.g., irritation increases corpuscle flow and adherence in living capillaries but produces only physical effects post-mortem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine for features of vitality such as displacement and renewal of redness under pressure, increased flow and cohesion of corpuscles, and the character of vesicle contents (vital fibrino-albuminous solution coagulable by heat vs serous/gaseous post-mortem). Use magnification and bright light to discern subtle differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and site considerations for tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific timing and choice of site affect test validity: allow hours for respiratory equilibrium; perform circulatory tests over the heart as primary site and corroborate on other trunk parts since heart area retains warmth longest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respiratory (CO2) test requires waiting a few hours to avoid misleading equilibrium effects. Circulatory/heat tests should prioritize the region over the heart but include corroborative areas. Use multiple tests and sites to exclude localized occlusion or artifacts (e.g., ligatured limb).
